subject: Mathematics
title: Arun and Priya's Market Day Mystery
hook: Arun needs to count 40 mangoes fast. Priya shows him a shortcut.

slides.title: The Mango Basket Problem
slides.storyContext: Arun's father owns a fruit shop. Today he received 4 baskets of mangoes, with 8 mangoes in each basket. Arun tries counting on his fingers but gets confused. Priya arrives to help.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Sunday morning at Delhi fruit market. Baskets stacked near the shop counter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun counts 4 baskets with 8 mangoes each.

slides.title: Groups and Repeated Addition
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Instead of counting 8 + 8 + 8 + 8, we can say 4 groups of 8. That's 4 times 8.'

points.label: Idea
points.text: Multiplication means: equal groups of things

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 4 × 8 means 4 groups of 8

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication is quick repeated addition of groups.

slides.title: Arun's Mango Count
slides.storyContext: Priya draws 4 circles, puts 8 dots in each. 'See? Add them all: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32. Or say 4 × 8 = 32.'

example.problem: 4 baskets, 8 mangoes each. How many total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Four times eight equals thirty-two mangoes total.

slides.title: Times Tables Start Here
slides.storyContext: Arun learns: 4 × 1 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 4 × 3 = 12... Priya says, 'It's like counting by 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20...'

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Multiplying by 4: skip count 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32...

slides.inSimpleWords: Times tables are skip counting in equal groups.

slides.title: Priya's Flower Pots
slides.storyContext: Priya mentions her garden: 'I have 6 pots with 3 flowers each. How many flowers do I have?'

example.problem: 6 pots with 3 flowers per pot. Total flowers?

slides.inSimpleWords: Six times three is eighteen flowers in total.

slides.title: Market Challenge
slides.storyContext: Arun's father asks: 'Arun, if I sell 5 bundles of 7 apples each, how many apples do I sell?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use groups: five groups of seven equals thirty-five.

slides.title: Order Doesn't Matter
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: '4 × 8 is the same as 8 × 4. Both give 32. You can flip the groups around.'

example.solution: Yes! Both = 15. Order of multiplication doesn't change the answer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the numbers; multiplication answer stays same.

slides.title: More Baskets Arrive
slides.storyContext: Suddenly, Arun's father gets a delivery: 3 more baskets, each with 10 mangoes! Arun says, 'That's 3 × 10. Can I use the same trick?'

points.label: New problem
points.text: Additional delivery: 3 baskets × 10 mangoes = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: Three baskets of ten mangoes—use multiplication again.

slides.title: Multiplying by 10 is Easy
slides.storyContext: Priya smiles: 'Watch! 1 × 10 = 10, 2 × 10 = 20, 3 × 10 = 30. When you multiply by 10, just add a zero!'

points.label: Rule
points.text: To multiply by 10, add a zero to the number

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplying by ten adds a zero to the end.

slides.title: Applying the Tens Rule
slides.storyContext: Arun counts: 3 × 10 = 30 mangoes, quick! Priya adds: 4 × 10 = 40, 6 × 10 = 60. They use the rule every time.
slides.inSimpleWords: Nine times ten equals ninety using the zero rule.

slides.title: Priya's Organizing Plan
slides.storyContext: Priya suggests: 'Let's arrange all the mangoes by type. We need to count different groups: red mangoes, yellow mangoes, green mangoes.'

points.label: Task
points.text: Sort and count mangoes by color using groups

slides.inSimpleWords: Counting different types of objects in groups.

slides.title: Two-Step Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Arun counts: 2 types × 4 baskets per type × 5 mangoes per basket. Priya says, 'Start with two groups of four: 2 × 4 = 8. Then 8 × 5 = 40.'

points.label: Strategy
points.text: Multiply step by step when working with many groups

slides.inSimpleWords: Break big multiplications into smaller steps.

slides.title: Sorting the Mangoes
slides.storyContext: Arun organizes: 'Red mangoes: 3 baskets × 6 per basket = 18. Yellow: 2 × 7 = 14. Green: 5 × 4 = 20. Total: 18 + 14 + 20 = 52.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each group, then add all results together.

slides.title: Double-Basket Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father sends word: He has 4 delivery trucks, each with 8 baskets, and each basket holds 6 mangoes. 'How many mangoes total?' Arun thinks hard.

points.label: Try this
points.text: 4 × 8 × 6 = ? (Hint: Do 4 × 8 first, then multiply by 6)

slides.inSimpleWords: Four trucks, eight baskets per truck, six mangoes per basket.

slides.title: Market Goes Real-World
slides.storyContext: By afternoon, the fruit shop is busy. Customers buy in multiples: 'Give me 3 bags of mangoes!' Arun realizes he uses multiplication every minute.

points.label: Real use
points.text: Customers ask for bundles, groups, and sets all day

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication helps count quick sales at the market.

slides.title: Multiplying by Doubles (2, 4, 8)
slides.storyContext: A customer asks: 'How much if I buy 2 bags? 4 bags? 8 bags?' Priya notices: 'Doubling is like going 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. Watch: 3 × 2 = 6, 3 × 4 = 12, 3 × 8 = 24. Double the number, double the answer!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplying by 2, 4, or 8 shows a doubling pattern.

slides.title: Quick Customer Service
slides.storyContext: Customer: 'I want 5 mangoes times 2 bags!' Arun: '5 × 2 = 10.' Customer: 'Then 5 × 4 bags!' Arun: '5 × 4 = 20. That's just 10 doubled!'

example.problem: A customer wants 7 apples × 2 times, then 7 × 4 times. What's each amount?
example.solution: 7 × 2 = 14 apples first time; 7 × 4 = 28 apples second time (14 doubled)

slides.inSimpleWords: When the multiplier doubles, the answer doubles too.

slides.title: The Ones and Nines Times Tables
slides.storyContext: Arun learns two easy tables: 'Times 1 is always the same: 1 × 5 = 5, 1 × 8 = 8. Times 9 is trickier: 1 × 9 = 9, 2 × 9 = 18, 3 × 9 = 27...'

points.label: Times 1
points.text: Any number × 1 = that same number

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplying by 1 gives the same number; times 9 follows a finger pattern.

image.alt: The Ones and Nines Times Tables — Multiplication

slides.title: Using the Ones and Nines Rules
slides.storyContext: Arun practices: '7 × 1 = 7 (easy!), 9 × 5 = 45 (use fingers).' Priya says, 'Ones are instant. Nines have a neat trick!'

example.solution: 3 × 1 = 3 (anything × 1 is itself); 9 × 6 = 54 (9 × 6: first digit 5 = 6-1, second digit 4 = 10-6)

slides.inSimpleWords: Ones are instant; nines follow the 9-digit sum pattern.

image.alt: Using the Ones and Nines Rules — Multiplication

slides.title: Practice Problems
slides.storyContext: Arun's father gives him homework: 'Count fast without mistakes.' Arun practices different multiplications with Priya helping.

points.label: Work
points.text: Practice builds speed and confidence with times tables

slides.inSimpleWords: Practicing multiplication helps you get faster.

slides.title: Real-Life Multiplication All Around
slides.storyContext: Priya points out: 'Multiplication is everywhere! Recipe calls for 3 batches of 4 eggs = 12 total. A school has 5 classes with 20 students = 100 students. A calendar: 7 days × 4 weeks = 28 days a month.'

points.label: Kitchen
points.text: Cooking: multiply ingredients by number of batches

points.label: School
points.text: Counting students: classes × students per class

points.label: Time
points.text: Calendar: days × weeks, weeks × months

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication appears in cooking, school, calendars, and money.

slides.title: Final Market Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arun's father leaves a final challenge: 'I received 6 shipments. Each shipment has 8 crates. Each crate has 5 kilos of mangoes. How many kilos total?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 6 × 8 × 5 = ? (work step by step)

slides.inSimpleWords: Six shipments, eight crates per shipment, five kilos each.

slides.title: Speed and Accuracy
slides.storyContext: By evening, Arun counts baskets with both speed AND accuracy. Priya challenges him: 'Can you multiply mentally? Not on paper?'

points.label: Skill
points.text: Mental multiplication comes with practice and pattern recognition

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular practice makes multiplication automatic and fast.

slides.title: Breaking Down Larger Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arun learns: 13 × 4 = (10 + 3) × 4 = (10 × 4) + (3 × 4) = 40 + 12 = 52. Split big numbers into tens and ones!

points.label: Method
points.text: Split numbers by place value: 13 = 10 + 3

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand numbers into tens and ones, multiply separately.

slides.title: Splitting Makes Bigger Multiplications Easy
slides.inSimpleWords: Split tens from ones, multiply each part separately.

image.alt: Splitting Makes Bigger Multiplications Easy — Multiplication

slides.title: Master-Level Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Arun's father gives him the hardest challenge: 'Multiply 32 × 6 without paper. Use what Priya taught you!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Apply splitting strategy to solve challenging multiplications.

slides.title: Arun's Journey Complete
slides.storyContext: By sunset, Arun realizes: multiplication isn't magic, it's patterns and shortcuts. From counting mangoes to mental math, he's grown into a multiplication master!

points.label: Growth
points.text: From confusion to confidence: repeated practice unlocks mastery

slides.inSimpleWords: Master multiplication through practice, patterns, and persistence.

slides.title: Arun Masters Multiplication
slides.storyContext: By evening, Arun counts every basket using multiplication. 'Thank you, Priya!' he says. 'Math is like a shortcut at the market!'

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiplication = equal groups added fast

points.label: Remember
points.text: 4 × 8 means 4 groups of 8

points.label: Remember
points.text: 4 × 8 = 8 × 4 (order doesn't matter)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Any number × 10 = add a zero

points.label: Remember
points.text: Double the multiplier = double the answer

points.label: Remember
points.text: × 1 gives the same number; × 9 uses finger tricks

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiplication is used in shopping, cooking, school, and calendars

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication makes counting groups quick and easy.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Birthday Cake Puzzle
hook: Priya has 24 candies to share fairly. Arun helps her divide them equally.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: birthday girl with a math puzzle

slides.title: Birthday Party Fair Share
slides.storyContext: Priya's birthday party has 24 chocolates. She wants to give each friend the same number. There are 6 friends (including her). How many chocolates does each friend get? Arun says, 'That's division!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Priya's home in Mumbai. Colorful table with 24 chocolates piled up.

slides.inSimpleWords: Priya divides chocolates equally among six friends.

slides.title: Division Means Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun explains: 'Division is the opposite of multiplication. Instead of 6 groups of 4, we ask: 24 things in 6 equal groups—how many in each?'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 24 ÷ 6 means 24 split into 6 equal groups

slides.inSimpleWords: Division shares things equally into groups.

slides.title: Sharing the Chocolates
slides.storyContext: Priya makes 6 piles of chocolates, one for each friend. She places them one by one in a circle: first friend, second friend, third... round and round until all 24 are placed.

example.problem: 24 chocolates shared equally among 6 friends. How many per friend?

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty-four divided by six equals four chocolates.

slides.title: Division and Multiplication are Opposites
slides.storyContext: Arun says: 'If 6 × 4 = 24, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Multiplication groups; division ungroups.'

points.label: Connection
points.text: 6 groups of 4 → multiply: 6 × 4 = 24

points.label: Connection
points.text: 24 things in 6 groups → divide: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 each

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication and division are opposite operations.

image.alt: Division and Multiplication are Opposites — Division

slides.title: Fruit Baskets
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Arun: 'My father packed 20 oranges into 5 baskets equally. How many oranges in each?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty oranges in five baskets equals four each.

slides.title: Division in the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother made 15 rotlis for dinner. The family has 3 people. How many rotlis per person if shared equally?
slides.inSimpleWords: Fifteen divided by three equals five rotlis each.

slides.title: Grouping Instead of Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun shows another way: 'We have 12 pencils. If we make groups of 3, how many groups?' He counts: 3, 6, 9, 12—that's 4 groups of 3.

example.problem: 12 pencils grouped in bundles of 3. How many bundles?

slides.inSimpleWords: Twelve pencils in groups of three make four.

slides.title: Guests Keep Arriving
slides.storyContext: More friends arrive! Now there are 8 friends total. Priya needs to divide 32 candies equally. 'How do we split 32 by 8?' Arun thinks of the times table.

points.label: New problem
points.text: 32 candies ÷ 8 friends = ? candies per friend

slides.inSimpleWords: Thirty-two candies shared fairly among eight friends.

slides.title: Division by Times Tables
slides.storyContext: Priya reminds Arun: 'Remember 8 times tables? 8 × 1 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, 8 × 3 = 24, 8 × 4 = 32. So 32 ÷ 8 = 4!' Division is the reverse lookup.

points.label: Method
points.text: To divide, think: What number times 8 equals 32?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use times tables backward to solve division problems.

slides.title: Candies Split Perfectly
slides.storyContext: Arun counts out: 4 candies for friend 1, 4 for friend 2, all the way to friend 8. Each gets exactly 4. 'Perfect! 32 ÷ 8 = 4!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Each of eight friends gets four candies exactly.

slides.title: Leftover Problem
slides.storyContext: Later, Priya finds 14 balloons to give to 3 friends. 'If I divide equally, do they each get the same?' Arun divides: 14 ÷ 3 = 4 with 2 left over.

points.label: New concept
points.text: Sometimes there's a remainder—not everything divides perfectly

slides.inSimpleWords: Division doesn't always divide evenly—sometimes there's a remainder.

slides.title: Remainders in Division
slides.storyContext: Arun explains: '14 balloons to 3 friends: 3 × 4 = 12, with 2 left. So 14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2 (4 remainder 2). Not perfect, but we tried!'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2 means 4 full groups and 2 left over

points.label: Check
points.text: (4 × 3) + 2 = 12 + 2 = 14 (matches original)

slides.inSimpleWords: Remainders are what's left when division isn't exact.

slides.title: Balloons and Remainders
slides.storyContext: Priya gives 4 balloons to each of 3 friends (12 total). She keeps 2 balloons for herself as extras. 'That works: 14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2.'

example.problem: 14 balloons shared among 3 friends. Each gets how many, with how many left?

slides.inSimpleWords: Four balloons each, with two extras remaining.

slides.title: Birthday Cake Portions
slides.storyContext: Priya's cake has 20 slices. There are 6 friends. 'How many slices each, and how many left for me?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 20 ÷ 6 = ? (Think: how many 6s in 20, and what's left?)

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty cake slices divided among six friends.

slides.title: Division Tricks from School
slides.storyContext: Arun recalls his teacher's tricks: 'Dividing by 2 means cut in half. Dividing by 10 means drop the zero. Dividing by 5 means... half of 10!'

points.label: Shortcut
points.text: Some divisions have special rules to make them faster

slides.inSimpleWords: Division tricks make hard problems quick to solve.

slides.title: Quick Division: Dividing by 2, 5, 10
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches fast division: 'Dividing by 2 is half. 20 ÷ 2 = 10. Dividing by 10 drops the zero. 30 ÷ 10 = 3. Dividing by 5 is half of dividing by 10. 30 ÷ 5 = 6.'

points.label: Rule
points.text: ÷ 2 = split in half

points.label: Rule
points.text: ÷ 10 = drop the zero from the end

points.label: Rule
points.text: ÷ 5 = divide by 10, then double the answer

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing by 2, 5, and 10 follow special shortcut rules.

slides.title: Fast Birthday Arithmetic
slides.storyContext: Priya checks: 40 guests ÷ 10 tables = 4 per table (drop the zero). 30 candies ÷ 5 bags = 6 per bag (divide by 10 = 3, double = 6).
slides.inSimpleWords: Shortcuts make division problems instant to answer.

slides.title: Real-Life Division
slides.storyContext: Priya spots division everywhere: 'Sharing snacks, dividing game teams, splitting the bill at restaurants, making equal portions for recipes!'

points.label: Real use
points.text: Fair sharing, sports teams, shopping, and cooking

slides.inSimpleWords: Division is used in real life to share and split fairly.

slides.title: Division and Grouping Compared
slides.storyContext: Arun learns two ways to think about division: (1) Sharing: 24 candies split among 6 friends = 4 each. (2) Grouping: How many groups of 6 are in 24? Answer: 4 groups.

points.label: Sharing model
points.text: Distribute items equally to a known number of groups

points.label: Grouping model
points.text: Count how many groups of a given size fit into a total

slides.inSimpleWords: Division can mean sharing or counting groups.

slides.title: Final Party Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father asks: 'We have 48 laddoos. We want to pack them in boxes of 8. How many boxes do we need?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 48 ÷ 8 = ? (using the grouping model)

slides.inSimpleWords: Forty-eight laddoos packed in groups of eight.

slides.title: Checking Your Answer
slides.storyContext: Arun learns an important trick: 'After I divide, I can multiply back to check. If 24 ÷ 6 = 4, then 4 × 6 should equal 24. It does!'

points.label: Check
points.text: Multiply your answer by the divisor to verify

slides.inSimpleWords: Check division answers by multiplying back.

slides.title: Unequal Sharing and Real-World Problems
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother has 13 cookies. We cannot divide 13 equally by 4. The family realizes unequal sharing happens in real life. 13 ÷ 4 = 3 R1.

points.label: Reality
points.text: Not all numbers divide evenly—real life is not always perfect

points.label: Three options
points.text: (1) Someone gets an extra item (2) Need more groups (3) Express as remainder or fraction

slides.inSimpleWords: Handle remainders by rounding, sharing extras, or using fractions.

image.alt: Unequal Sharing and Real-World Problems — Division

slides.title: Real Remainders in Action
slides.storyContext: Arun: 17 cookies for 5 friends. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 R2. Give 3 to each friend, 2 friends get an extra. Or give 3 to all and keep 2.

example.problem: Share 25 apples among 6 people. Express as quotient and remainder.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use quotient and remainder to describe unequal sharing.

slides.title: Master-Level Division Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's father challenges: 'We have 89 guests. We need to arrange them into tables of 7. How many tables, and how many at the odd table?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 89 ÷ 7 = 12 R5 (12 full tables of 7, one table with 5 guests)

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply division with remainders to real event-planning problems.

slides.title: Division Powers the Real World
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes: Division is everywhere—splitting bills, arranging seats, scheduling shifts, packing boxes. Without division, shared living doesn't work!

points.label: Impact
points.text: Division enables fairness, organization, and planning in daily life

slides.inSimpleWords: Division is essential for fair sharing and organizing groups.

image.alt: Division Powers the Real World — Division

slides.title: Party Success with Division
slides.storyContext: Each friend gets exactly what they need. Priya smiles. 'Arun, division makes sure everyone gets the same. Fair and square!'

points.label: Remember
points.text: Division shares things equally or makes equal groups

points.label: Remember
points.text: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 means 24 things in 6 equal parts

points.label: Remember
points.text: Division is the opposite of multiplication

points.label: Remember
points.text: Some divisions leave a remainder (not perfect)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Quick tricks: ÷2 halves, ÷10 drops zero, ÷5 is half

points.label: Remember
points.text: Two models: sharing (divide among groups) and grouping (count groups)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Check by multiplying: quotient × divisor = dividend

slides.inSimpleWords: Division ensures fair, equal sharing among everyone.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun and Priya's Pizza Party
hook: One pizza. Two friends. How do they split it fairly?

slides.title: Cutting the Pizza
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya order one pizza. Arun cuts it straight down the middle. 'Now each of us gets one half,' says Priya. 'That's a fraction!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Pizza place in Bangalore. One round pizza, knife, two hungry kids.

slides.inSimpleWords: One pizza cut into two equal halves for sharing.

slides.title: What is a Fraction?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'A fraction is a part of a whole. When we cut the pizza into 2 equal pieces, each piece is 1/2 of the pizza. Numerator (top) is how many pieces. Denominator (bottom) is total pieces.'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 1/2 means 1 out of 2 equal pieces

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Top number = how many pieces you have

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Bottom number = total pieces in the whole

slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows parts of one whole thing.

slides.title: Halves (1/2)
slides.storyContext: Arun takes one half. Priya takes the other half. Together, 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 whole pizza.

example.problem: One pizza cut into 2 equal halves. Arun eats 1 half. How much of the whole?

slides.inSimpleWords: Each half is one out of two equal pieces.

slides.title: Thirds (1/3)
slides.storyContext: Next day, Arun, Priya, and Arun's brother come. One pizza. Three friends. 'Cut it into thirds,' says Arun. Each friend gets 1/3 of the pizza.

points.label: Thirds
points.text: 1/3 means 1 out of 3 equal pieces

points.label: Picture
points.text: Pizza divided into 3 equal slices

slides.inSimpleWords: Thirds divide something equally into three pieces.

slides.title: Three Friends, Three Thirds Pizza
slides.storyContext: Priya eats 1/3 of the pizza. Arun eats 1/3. Arun's brother eats 1/3. Together: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = the whole pizza.

example.problem: One pizza divided into 3 equal pieces. Each friend gets how much?
example.solution: Each friend gets 1/3 of the pizza

slides.inSimpleWords: Three equal thirds make one complete whole pizza.

image.alt: Three Friends, Three Thirds Pizza — Fractions

slides.title: Quarters (1/4)
slides.storyContext: A week later, Arun, Priya, and two more friends meet. 'Four friends, one pizza,' says Arun. They cut it into 4 equal squares. Each gets 1/4.

points.label: Quarters
points.text: 1/4 means 1 out of 4 equal pieces

slides.inSimpleWords: Quarters split something into four equal parts.

slides.title: Chocolate Bar Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun has a chocolate bar with 8 squares. He gives Priya 2 squares. What fraction did he give her?

points.label: Try this
points.text: 2 out of 8 squares = 2/8. Can you simplify it?

slides.inSimpleWords: Two out of eight equals one fourth of chocolate.

slides.title: Comparing Slice Sizes
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: 'If I eat 1/2 of a pizza, I eat way more than 1/4. And way more than 1/8. Bigger fractions have smaller denominators!'

points.label: Observation
points.text: 1/2 is bigger than 1/4, which is bigger than 1/8

slides.inSimpleWords: Bigger denominators mean smaller pieces.

slides.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arun draws pizzas: one cut in 2 (halves), one in 4 (quarters), one in 8 (eighths). 'Look! Each piece gets smaller as we divide more.'

points.label: Rule
points.text: Fraction with BIGGER denominator = SMALLER pieces

points.label: Order
points.text: 1/2 > 1/4 > 1/8 (biggest to smallest)

slides.inSimpleWords: More pieces means each piece is smaller.

slides.title: Which is Bigger?
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Would you rather eat 1/2 of a pizza or 1/3?' Arun thinks: 'Half, because halves are bigger pieces than thirds!'

example.solution: 1/2 is bigger (two halves make whole, three thirds make whole; halves are bigger pieces)

slides.inSimpleWords: Half of pizza is bigger than one third of pizza.

slides.title: Mixed Up Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arun eats 1/4 of a pizza, then 1/4 again. Priya says, 'That's 2/4! That's the same as 1/2!' Arun realizes fractions can be written different ways.

points.label: Discovery
points.text: 2/4 of pizza = 1/2 of pizza. Same amount, different names!

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can represent the same amount.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya draws: 1/2 pizza cut into 2 pieces, then the SAME pizza cut into 4 pieces and shading 2. 'See? 1/2 = 2/4. Same pizza, cut different ways!'

points.label: Rule
points.text: Multiply or divide numerator AND denominator by the same number

points.label: Example
points.text: 1/2 × 2/2 = 2/4 (same value, bigger numbers)

slides.inSimpleWords: Equivalent fractions look different but mean the same.

slides.title: Finding Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arun starts: 1/3. He doubles top and bottom: 2/6. He triples: 3/9. 'All the same slice size, just more pieces!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply top and bottom by same number for equivalent fractions.

slides.title: Simplifying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 4/8 of a cake. 'Can I simplify this?' Arun says, 'Divide top and bottom by 2: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2. That's simpler!'

points.label: Try this
points.text: Simplify 6/8. Hint: Divide both by 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide top and bottom by same number to simplify.

slides.title: Adding Fractions with Same Denominator
slides.storyContext: Priya eats 1/4 of a pizza. Then she eats 2/4 more. 'How much total?' Arun counts: '1 + 2 = 3 pieces out of 4. That's 3/4!'

points.label: Pattern
points.text: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4 (same denominator, add numerators)

slides.inSimpleWords: When denominators match, add numerators only.

image.alt: Adding Fractions with Same Denominator — Fractions

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arun learns: 'If fractions have the SAME denominator, just add the numerators. Don't change the denominator!' He practices: 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Same denominator? Add numerators: a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c

slides.inSimpleWords: Add numerators when denominators are the same.

slides.title: Pizza Arithmetic
slides.storyContext: Priya: '1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 of one pizza.' Arun: 'And 5/8 - 2/8 = 3/8 of another!' They solve quickly using the rule.
slides.inSimpleWords: Practice adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions.

slides.title: Fractions in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Priya points out: 'Fractions are everywhere! Half a glass of milk, quarter hour on the clock, third of a cake, two-thirds full tank of petrol.'

points.label: Real use
points.text: Time (1/4 hour), volume (1/2 cup), temperature, cooking recipes

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole in daily life.

slides.title: Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arun gets confused: 'What if I eat 5/4 of a pizza? That's more than one whole!' Priya explains: '5/4 is called an improper fraction. It means 1 and 1/4 pizzas, or 1 1/4.'

points.label: Improper fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ denominator (5/4, 3/2, 7/5)

points.label: Mixed number
points.text: Whole number + fraction (1 1/4, 2 3/5)

points.label: Conversion
points.text: 5/4 = 1 1/4 (divide 5 by 4: quotient 1, remainder 1)

slides.inSimpleWords: Improper fractions have numerators bigger than or equal to denominators.

image.alt: Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers — Fractions

slides.title: Converting Mixed Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arun converts: '1 1/2 pizzas = ? Multiply 1 × 2 = 2, add the 1: (2+1)/2 = 3/2. So 1 1/2 = 3/2!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions by multiplying.

slides.title: Final Pizza Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father brings a surprise: '2 pizzas cut into quarters. You have already eaten 5 quarters. How much pizza is left as a fraction?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 2 pizzas = 8 quarters. 8/4 - 5/4 = ? or 3/4 left?

slides.inSimpleWords: Two pizzas have eight quarters total; find the leftover amount.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'Is 1/2 bigger than 2/5?' Arun draws both and realizes he needs a common denominator to compare fairly.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Comparing 1/2 and 2/5 requires different approach

points.label: Solution
points.text: Convert to common denominator: 1/2 = 5/10 and 2/5 = 4/10

slides.inSimpleWords: Use common denominators to compare different fractions.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators — Fractions

slides.title: Converting to Compare
slides.storyContext: Priya practices: Compare 1/3 and 1/4. Common denominator is 12. 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12. So 1/3 > 1/4.
slides.inSimpleWords: Convert both fractions to same denominator, then compare numerators.

slides.title: Master-Level Fraction Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's big challenge: 'I ate 1/3 of a pizza Monday, 1/4 of a pizza Tuesday. How much pizza did I eat in total?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 1/3 + 1/4: common denominator is 12. 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12. Total = 7/12 pizza

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions with different denominators by finding common denominator.

slides.title: Fractions Build Confidence
slides.storyContext: By week's end, Arun and Priya spot fractions everywhere with confidence. Music (3/4 time), recipes (1/2 cup), sports (first quarter), clocks (quarter past)—fractions unlock understanding!

points.label: Mastery
points.text: Fractions are the foundation for deeper math like algebra and percentages

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions connect to music, time, cooking, and advanced math.

slides.title: Fractions Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Arun and Priya see fractions all around: half a glass of milk, a quarter hour on the clock, three-quarters of a tank full.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Fraction = one or more equal parts of a whole

points.label: Remember
points.text: 1/2 (half), 1/3 (third), 1/4 (quarter) are common

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bottom number = how many equal pieces total

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bigger denominator = smaller each piece

points.label: Remember
points.text: Same denominator? Add numerators, keep denominator same

points.label: Remember
points.text: Equivalent fractions look different but mean the same

points.label: Remember
points.text: Improper fractions (5/4) can be written as mixed numbers (1 1/4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole in daily life.
